title: the Gayatri in context
hook: a laptop clicks shut, a shop pulls down its shutter. a Vedic poet gave that hour a god

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context: one verse inside a hymn that turns from god to god, the first verse to Savitr. Did you go looking for what came before and after a line? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

Six in the evening. A laptop lid clicks shut. Down the block, a shop owner rattles the shutter down over the window. A bus fills with people carrying bags, heading home. Somewhere a pot goes on the stove. Nobody announced it, but the day has turned, and everyone is stopping at once. A Vedic poet watched this same hour and gave it a god. It's the god the Gayatri speaks to. Today: who Savitr is, in the hymns that sing about him.
screen: `A LAPTOP CLICKS SHUT.` → `EVERYONE STOPS AT ONCE.` → `THE POET GAVE THE HOUR A GOD.`

segments.voice: The Gayatri asks one thing of Savitr: may he stir our thoughts. To hear that request fully, it helps to meet Savitr in the other hymns. In the Rig Veda he is pictured in gold. One hymn calls him hiranyapani, golden-handed, a god who comes on a shining chariot and looks over the creatures of the world. He's the sun, but more than the ball of light. He's the power that sets things going. Then there's a hymn in book two that sees him at the other end of the day. When Savitr comes at evening, it says, in paraphrase, the weaver rolls up the cloth she was weaving. The worker sets down a task half done. The one who was traveling turns toward home. The birds go back to their nests. Everything that was moving comes to rest, because Savitr has said so. So Savitr isn't only the god of starting. He's the god of the whole swing of the day: the stirring in the morning and the stopping at night. He sends people out, and he calls them home. That changes how the Gayatri's request sounds. Asking this god to stir the mind isn't asking for endless motion. It's asking the one who knows when to begin and when to stop. The weaver in that hymn doesn't finish her row. She rolls up the cloth because the hour has come, and the cloth will be there tomorrow.
screen: `THE GAYATRI SPEAKS TO SAVITR.` · `GOLDEN-HANDED, IN THE HYMNS.` · `AT EVENING, THE WEAVER ROLLS UP HER CLOTH.` · `THE ONE WHO STIRS, AND THE ONE WHO STILLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stir, then still. Sit, and for the first part of the sit, let the breath be a little fuller, as if the day were starting. Notice the body waking: the hands, the shoulders, the face. Then, halfway through, let the breath go back to its own pace. Picture rolling up one piece of today's work, unfinished, and setting it aside. Not dropping it. Rolling it up. If you pray, you can hold the Gayatri's meaning, may our thoughts be stirred, through both halves. The bell holds the time.
The Gayatri in context. The god it speaks to is Savitr: golden-handed, the one who sets the day moving and, at evening, lets it rest. Today's word.
Your line: the Gayatri in context. Tonight, at whatever hour your day turns, roll up one unfinished thing on purpose and leave it for tomorrow. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Hindus who keep sandhya recite the Gayatri at the day's turning points, dawn and dusk, so the verse to Savitr is said both as the day begins and as it closes.

original.note: Sanskrit: golden-handed, a name the Rig Veda gives Savitr.

trapdoor: what you thought: Savitr is the sunrise.
what it means: Savitr is the power that sets things moving, and in one hymn the one who brings them to rest at evening.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 2.38, the evening hymn to Savitr, with the weaver rolling up her cloth and work left half done.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.35 (Savitr, golden-handed, on his chariot)
Rig Veda 2.38 (Savitr at evening: the weaver, the half-done work, the traveler, the birds)

notes: hiranyapani (golden-handed) for Savitr: given from memory for Rig Veda 1.35 (around verse 9); confirm the verse.
Rig Veda 2.38 paraphrase (weaver rolls up her web, worker leaves work half done, traveler turns home, birds to nests) given from memory across verses 3–7; confirm each image is in the hymn.
The reading that Savitr is 'the god of the whole swing of the day' is an interpretive summary of these hymns, not a quotation.
The six o'clock scene is the writer's image, not the hymn's.
